contract_rules: Topics and state/attributes JSON keys are the contract surface. Adding a topic or a field is a minor bump (consumers ignore what they do not know); changing a key's meaning, removing one, or moving a topic is a major bump and requires the old and new form published in parallel for one major cycle. v1 freezes on the first public release; before that this file changes freely.
note: Contract between the bridge firmware and everything that consumes it (panel firmware, Home Assistant, Mi Home, Node-RED). Neither side imports the other's code; both are generated from or validated against this file.
device_id_note: Last 6 hex digits of the heater BLE address, lower case. Stable across reflashes, so entities survive a firmware update.
retain_policy: Retain status, never readings. A retained reading keeps answering from the broker after the bridge is gone, and any subscriber that does not also read `link` takes it for the truth; `state` and `attributes` are therefore live-only. Statuses are the opposite: `availability=offline` and `link=offline` are true statements about a bridge that stopped, and a consumer that restarts needs them without waiting. Nothing is lost by dropping state's retain flag - the bridge republishes on every A0 frame (~4 s) and every 60 s respectively, so a late consumer is one interval behind at worst. Home Assistant reaches the same conclusion for sensor state payloads (sensor.mqtt, `expire_after`): a broker replaying an expired value at startup is the failure to design out.

state.purpose: Full device snapshot, published on every A0 frame (~4 s) while the heater answers, and by the 60 s heartbeat only while the snapshot is still fresh. Live-only: a reading that survives the bridge that took it is a lie waiting for a subscriber, so this topic is never retained. A consumer that needs to know whether the values are current reads link; one that arrives while the bridge is down gets nothing, which is the intended answer.

availability.purpose: Liveness of the bridge itself, not of the data: 'online' means this process is running and talking to the broker. Last will is 'offline'. A consumer must treat a missing state plus 'offline' as unknown, not as zero. Freshness of the readings is a separate signal - see the link topic.

link.purpose: Freshness of the heater data, separate from the bridge being alive. 'online' while A0 frames keep arriving; the bridge publishes 'offline' after 90 s without one (22 missed frames at the 4 s cadence), and again on every reconnect until a new frame lands. Retained, so a consumer that restarts learns the current freshness instead of guessing. A consumer must combine it with availability, not substitute it: availability alone says the bridge is up, which is exactly the state in which it used to republish a two-day-old snapshot with a fresh heartbeat.

set_temperature.purpose: Setpoint. The bridge ignores out-of-range values rather than clamping.

command.purpose: Operational commands. 'refresh' asks for an immediate state publish.

ota.purpose: Firmware update URL, or the literal 'install' to flash the URL last seen on update/url. The bridge downloads the image over HTTP, flashes the inactive slot, validates, and reboots into it; on any failure the running firmware is untouched. http only (https has no TLS stack in the flasher path); port defaults to 80; a bare host without a path is refused. Delivery must be live - a retained URL would reflash the board on every reconnect, which is a boot loop that overwrites the firmware each time.

update_manifest_latest.purpose: Latest available firmware version, published by whoever owns the manifest (the bench tool today, a release pipeline later). Retained on purpose: a rebooted bridge learns the current manifest from the broker on its first subscribe, so the update entity never lies about what is available. Replaying it is idempotent state, not a command - this is the deliberate opposite of the live-only ota topic.

update_manifest_url.purpose: Firmware image URL backing the version on update/latest. Retained like update/latest: the bridge caches it and only ever flashes on an explicit live 'install'. A bad URL is refused by the same parser as the ota topic (rules::parseOtaUrl), so both paths share one grammar and one test suite.

update_state.purpose: The update entity's state: {"installed_version":...,"latest_version":...}. latest_version is omitted entirely until a manifest has been seen, so Home Assistant shows 'unknown' rather than a fake up-to-date. Republished on connect, on every manifest change, and on the 60 s heartbeat. Retained: it is status, so a consumer that restarts gets the current pair immediately instead of an 'unknown' card for a heartbeat; replaying it is idempotent.

attributes.purpose: Slow-changing metadata and link health: firmware version, heater address, uptime, BLE RSSI, last disconnect. Separate topic so it is not repeated in every state message; republished on every connect and once a minute, so uptime and RSSI age at most a minute. Live-only like state: uptime and RSSI are readings, and a retained uptime outlives the bridge that measured it.

state_fields.label: Active fault code
state_fields.note: Two upper-case hex digits, or 'none'. Never an empty string - a consumer drawing a fault badge needs a definite value.

state_fields.label: Bridge timestamp (epoch)
state_fields.note: Set by the bridge, not by the heater. Consumers detect a stalled bridge by an ageing ts.

attributes_fields.label: BLE signal strength
attributes_fields.note: null while the link is down or the radio refused a read - a real reading is always negative, so 0 would be a number nobody measured. Home Assistant renders null as unknown; do not substitute 0.

attributes_fields.label: Last MQTT disconnect reason
attributes_fields.note: Why the broker link last dropped ('tcp connect failed', 'no traffic in 90 s', ...). Survives the reconnect so a flapping link is visible while it is up. 'not started' before the first attempt.

attributes_fields.label: Last MQTT disconnect time
attributes_fields.note: null = the broker link has not dropped since boot. This is the broker link, not the BLE link. The wire value is epoch seconds - the label deliberately does not say so, because the Home Assistant entity renders ISO 8601: device_class timestamp parses ISO 8601 and rejects a bare integer, so the template formats with timestamp_custom. A label promising 'epoch' next to an ISO 8601 value is a small lie a user reads every time they open the device page.

device.identifiers_note: device_id already starts with 'btwh_', so prefixing it again would yield btwh_btwh_<last6>. The identifier is the device_id itself.
device.name: Water heater
device.version_note: sw_version is the @FW@ token, replaced by gen_ha.py with kFirmwareVersion read out of firmware/bridge/src/net/mqtt_client.h - so the device page cannot claim a version the board is not running, and --check fails when the header is older than a bump. hw_version is the build target, which is fixed for this firmware. Both belong here rather than on diagnostic sensors: Home Assistant shows them on the device page, and they describe the hardware, not a measurement.

home_assistant.entity_note: One entity per state field. Sensors use state_class measurement; setpoint is a number entity; flame is a binary_sensor; mode is an enum sensor; fault is a sensor with an icon template plus a problem binary_sensor (see fault_binary_sensor). Every attributes field is also an entity, but entity_category diagnostic, so Home Assistant files it under diagnostics instead of cluttering the device page - a remote user can read firmware, RSSI and the last disconnect without shell access to the board.

fault_binary_sensor.name: Fault active
fault_binary_sensor.note: The string sensor keeps the code ('E9', 'none'); this second entity answers the only question an automation asks: is something wrong right now. device_class problem is the community convention for that - it is what Home Assistant's UI highlights and what a trigger reads without a template. Two entities over one field rather than one entity doing both, because a sensor cannot also be a problem binary_sensor. The template defaults a missing field to 'none': the state payload always carries fault, and a binary_sensor that rendered None (or an empty string) would log 'Invalid state message' instead of showing anything.

origin.name: btwh-bridge
origin.note: Discovery provenance. Home Assistant recommends it for single-component discovery and requires it for device discovery; it is what the core log prints when an entity is discovered. sw_version is left out here on purpose - the version belongs to the device map (device.sw_version), which Home Assistant renders on the device page; repeating it in origin would be a third copy of the same number. support_url points at the repository; keep it only while that URL resolves, a dead support link is worse than none.

availability_rule.note: A state-derived entity (measurements and the water_heater view) is only as good as the freshest frame: it binds both topics with availability_mode all, so losing the heater greys it out instead of showing a number nobody measured. A bridge-derived entity (the attributes diagnostics and the update entity) binds availability only - pairing state, RSSI and 'install firmware' are facts about the bridge and must stay readable precisely when the heater is unreachable. Single-topic entities keep using availability_topic; the list form appears only where a second topic is added, because the two forms are mutually exclusive.

birth.note: Home Assistant's own birth/will topic. Its MQTT integration publishes 'online' there when it starts, so a bridge that hears it can repair a consumer that restarted with nothing cached: discovery is retained and reloaded from the broker anyway, but attributes and state are live-only (see retain_policy), so without this message a restarted Home Assistant would show blank diagnostics until the next 60 s heartbeat. The topic is Home Assistant's fixed default, not derived from discovery_prefix - it is not a place this bridge publishes anything, only subscribes. 'offline' is ignored: the bridge keeps publishing either way, and a retained discovery document is what gets the next start up.

update_entity.title: BTWH Bridge
update_entity.note: The HA update entity: installed_version comes from the firmware itself, latest_version from the retained manifest topics (update/latest + update/url). Clicking Install in HA publishes 'install' to the existing ota topic - the same live-only path the bench tool uses, so there is exactly one flasher and one grammar. The bridge mediates the state (rather than HA reading the manifest topics directly) because the install command needs the URL cached on the board anyway. Version strings are compared as strings by HA; dev suffixes like '-ota2' are bench-only - release builds must use plain semver. No entity_category: an update is a primary control, and 'config' would bury the Install button in the section nobody opens.

water_heater_entity.note: Home Assistant's water_heater domain is how the heater stops being 'a pile of sensors' and becomes a first-class heater: dedicated card, voice control semantics, energy panel, and the Matter/HomeKit bridging Home Assistant already provides. All topics reuse the v1 contract - nothing moves, this is purely an adapter view. mode has no command topic because a tankless heater has no switchable mode; 'gas' means the burner is firing, 'off' means idle. temperature_unit is 'C' because the water_heater MQTT schema takes C/F, not the degree sign the sensor schema demands - the two whitelists differ.

consumer_rules: A missing field means 'not reported yet'; a null field means 'reported, but unknown right now' (rssi with the link down, last_disconnect_at before the first drop). Do not print either as 0 - an unheated heater and an unreachable bridge must look different.
fault == 'none' is healthy; any other value is a fault code, not text.
availability == 'offline' overrides state: show 'unavailable' and stop drawing the last value as current.

state and attributes are live-only. A consumer that starts while the bridge is down receives nothing, and that is the correct answer - do not fill the gap with a local cache and present it as current. Hold the last value only as long as you also hold the fact that it is old.
Never hard-code the base topic in firmware: generate it from this file or read it from the bridge's attributes.

producers.python/tools/: a reference publisher, useful when testing a panel without a bridge

consumers.firmware/panel/: planned touch panel; generates its UI binding from state_fields
consumers.integrations/homeassistant/: planned integration; generates entities from the same list
consumers.firmware/bridge/: publishes; must pass the contract test before release

source_of_truth: state_fields keys are checked against python/bosch_api.py::DeviceState by python/tests/test_mqtt_contract.py; renaming a field there without updating this file fails CI.
